chapter_theme: Punavayil (புனவாயில்): one song of the death-bed, speech gone, eyes dim, milk spilling from the mouth, the physician giving up and wives and kin falling and wailing, with the plea that on the day Death comes Murugan appear with the peacock, his twelve arms and his two consorts; the praise tells of Hanuman bringing Sita's tokens to Rama, whose nephew dwells at Punavayil.

1325.reading: The poet pictures his own death: speech gone, tongue dry, eyes like cotton, the milk given him standing and dribbling from the corner of the mouth, the body chilled, hands and legs stiff, flesh and belly shrunk, the physician saying no remedy will work now, kin and wives beating themselves and falling in tears; he asks that on the day Death comes to take his life Murugan appear before him with the peacock, the twelve strong arms, the garlands and his two consorts. The praise tells how Hanuman, son of the wind, brought tokens to Rama, and how Rama, seeing along the path Sita's earrings, ring, anklets, bracelets and the ball she had thrown, grieved; Murugan is Narayana's nephew at southern Punavayil.
1325.nuance: The death is told sign by sign from inside the dying body, then from the bedside: the physician's verdict (பரிகாரி வரவொன்றும் பலியாது இனி) and the women's wailing. The plea asks not to escape death but for a vision at the hour. In the praise Sita's ornaments scattered along the road are listed as fully as the dying body's signs; the reading of these lines is tentative.

links.note: Both mark the end by the physician giving up (Tirumular's lets go the pulse, 1325's says no remedy will work) while wife and wealth stay behind or wail; Tirumular leaves it there, while 1325 asks for Murugan to come at that hour.

source_issues: 1325: a line end is damaged ('....... ; யல்தோகை'), with syllables lost before the word for the peacock.
1325: a stray space after the vowel உ splits words at line starts (உ ரையும், உ லர்ந்தது, உ ழலும், உ டலும், உ றவும்); read as one word.
